name: Odeya Blouse (Adire Print)
description:
A loose, flowing blouse cut from a medium-weight fabric printed in a modern interpretation of traditional Yoruba adire resist-dyeing: deep indigo ground with irregular white geometric resists — circles, broken lines, scatter patterns — that look hand-done because they were, at least in the original design that the print is derived from. The silhouette is generous through the body with wide sleeves that taper at the wrist, a V-neckline, and a hem that falls to mid-hip. The fabric moves well and the color holds through washing.

Made by a small family label out of the Tier 2 textile district — Odeya has been producing adire-influenced pieces for three generations, adapting the patterns each decade while maintaining the visual language. The blouse is popular across Tiers 2 through 4, worn by people who appreciate heritage design and by people who simply think it's beautiful without knowing its context. Both are fine.
what_it_says: I carry something forward without making a speech about it.
worn_by: people with West African family heritage
story_hooks: The specific resist pattern on one blouse — an unusual variation — appears in a three-hundred-year-old photograph, raising questions about how the design survived.
Odeya's original pattern archive was stolen; the family is quietly trying to recover it before a corponation files a design patent on their own heritage.
A character receives this blouse as a gift from someone they've never met, with a note that says only: 'She would have wanted you to have it.'
